notes.title: Start here: the map, two traces, and the 29-line brain
notes.body:
astraboot1 is a learning platform: a React web app, a Fastify API, a Prisma/PostgreSQL schema, and a few shared packages. The docs are short and the code is dense, so read in this order:

1. `docs/codebase-tour.md`, the map. It names every folder and then walks two traces (completing a lesson, grading an attempt) that cross every layer.
2. `apps/api/src/db.ts`. The tour says to read its two helpers, `mutate` and `award`, before either trace. They are about twenty lines.
3. `docs/learning-algorithms.md`, which explains XP, the review scheduler, mastery and placement, all implemented in `packages/learning-core/src/index.ts`.
4. `docs/testing.md`, the verification record: what was actually run, and what is explicitly not claimed.

A tip from the tour itself: the API routes are written in a few very long lines. If one is hard to follow, paste it into a formatter in a scratch buffer. The behaviour lives in the order of the `await`s, not in the layout.

excerpts.quote: Read this map first, then walk the two traces below — they cross every layer the map names.
`apps/api/src/db.ts`: the two helpers everything else leans on — `mutate` (idempotency receipts) and `award` (unique XP). Nineteen lines; read them before either trace.

readMore.why: The folder map and the two end-to-end traces.
The rules for XP, scheduling, mastery and placement in plain words.

notes.title: Concept: replay-safe writes with mutate and award
notes.body:
Networks fail, and clients retry. The API protects every private write with two helpers in `db.ts`.

**mutate** wraps a write in one database transaction. It first locks the owner's `User` row with `FOR UPDATE`, so two writes for the same owner run one after the other. Then it looks for a **mutation receipt**: a stored record of an earlier request with the same `clientEventId`. The request body is hashed, and the receipt keeps that hash and the response that was sent. Read what `mutate` does in each case: no receipt, a receipt with the same hash, and a receipt with a different hash.

**award** grants XP with a database upsert. Read its `where` key and its `update` branch, then find how each route builds the `awardKey` it passes in (which parts of the item go into it).

These are two different safety nets. When a quiz asks why something happens only once, ask yourself which net caught it.

excerpts.quote: // All owner mutations serialize; this is small private-app traffic. Database constraints remain the final safeguard. await tx.$queryRaw`SELECT id FROM "User" WHERE id = ${userId}::uuid FOR UPDATE`;
- `apps/api/src/db.ts`: the two helpers everything else leans on — `mutate` (idempotency receipts) and `award` (unique XP). Nineteen lines; read them before either trace.

readMore.why: Both helpers in full; short enough to read in one sitting.

notes.title: Concept: the learning rules are pure functions
notes.body:
All the "learning brain" lives in one file, `packages/learning-core/src/index.ts`. Its functions take plain values and return plain values. They never read the database or the clock themselves; even the current time is passed in as `now`. That makes every rule deterministic and easy to test, and it lets the server's time stay authoritative.

Three functions matter most:

- `schedule(step, rating, correctness, now)` picks the next review step and due time. Steps index into a fixed list of day intervals.
- `conceptStatus(evidence, reviews, overdue)` decides whether a concept is unseen, practicing, demonstrated, retained or review_due. It filters the evidence first; note exactly which passes it keeps, and why.
- `placementOutcome(...)` decides whether a placement test lets a learner skip ahead.

Read each one slowly with the doc open beside it. The doc's prose and the one-line code should say the same thing; checking that they do is good practice in itself.

excerpts.quote: — 29 lines of pure functions with no imports beyond types. That's a deliberate boundary: the scheduler and graders take plain values (including `now: Date` as a parameter) and return plain values
export function schedule(step:number,rating:Rating,correctness:boolean|null,now:Date) {

notes.title: What a run with skipped integration suites proves
notes.body:
The integration suites are the tests that talk to a real PostgreSQL database. Without `TEST_DATABASE_URL` they are skipped. The rest of the suite may pass, but a skipped test checked nothing, so the run says **nothing** about whether data is really saved. The verification record states this in one line, right after the setup instructions: you must point both database variables at a disposable database and apply migrations before `pnpm test` counts as persistence evidence.

Why the others are wrong:
- **skipped counts as passing**: a skip is not a pass; the guide says skipped suites are not evidence.
- **reads proven, writes not**: neither is proven, because no database was touched at all.
- **proven if the Vite build passes**: a front-end build compiles code; it never touches the database.

excerpts.quote: Set `DATABASE_URL` and `TEST_DATABASE_URL` to the same dedicated disposable PostgreSQL database, apply migrations, then run `pnpm test`. Skipped integration suites are not persistence evidence.

notes.title: What moves a demonstrated concept to retained
notes.body:
After the demonstrated check, `conceptStatus` looks at reviews. It keeps only reviews that were **correct and due**, sorts them by time, and asks whether any pair falls on **different UTC dates** and is **at least seven days apart** (`7*86400000` milliseconds). If so, the concept is retained. The idea is that remembering something twice, a week apart, when it was actually due, is evidence that it stuck.

Why the others are wrong:
- **seven consecutive days, due or not**: the filter requires `r.due`; early reviews do not count, and a streak is not what is measured.
- **any two correct reviews on different dates**: different dates alone is not enough; the gap must also be at least seven days.
- **a third transfer-level pass**: retention is about reviews, not more exercise passes.

excerpts.quote: const good=reviews.filter(r=>r.correct&&r.due)
b.at.getTime()-a.at.getTime()>=7*86400000
**Retained** additionally requires two correct, due reviews on different UTC dates at least seven days apart.

notes.title: What evidence makes a concept demonstrated
notes.body:
`conceptStatus` first filters the evidence to **independent** passes: `passed`, `assistance === 'none'`, and `origin !== 'self_reported'`. Then two things must both be true: those passes cover at least **two distinct itemIds** (it builds a `Set` of ids), and at least one of them is at `apply`, `debug` or `transfer` level. Two different unassisted, non-self-reported passes with one at a higher level is exactly that.

Why the others are wrong:
- **two rubric items with selfAssessment true**: rubric grading records origin `self_reported`, which the filter removes.
- **one debug item on three days**: repeating the same item gives a `Set` of size one; distinct items are required.
- **two items passed after viewing the solution**: a reveal marks attempts `solution_viewed`, so assistance is not `none`.

excerpts.quote: const independent=evidence.filter(e=>e.passed && e.assistance==='none' && e.origin!=='self_reported'); const demonstrated=new Set(independent.map(e=>e.itemId)).size>=2 && independent.some(e=>['apply','debug','transfer'].includes(e.level));
`rubric` grading → `self_reported`

notes.title: Why a reset editor does not erase a reveal
notes.body:
Before grading, the attempt handler reads the `RevealEvent` rows for this item at this `masteryRevision`. If the solution was ever revealed, every later attempt is marked `solution_viewed`. Reveal history is a database table, not something kept in the browser, so clearing or resetting the editor changes nothing on the server. The tour says it plainly: resetting the editor does not reset evidence. The new attempt is recorded as `solution_viewed`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **reset clears the reveal**: the reset is UI state; the reveal is a stored row.
- **rejected outright**: the attempt is accepted and graded; it is only labelled as assisted.
- **unassisted after the next UTC day**: no rule ties reveals to dates; the tour calls the marking permanent at that revision.

excerpts.quote: if the solution was ever revealed, every later attempt is permanently marked `solution_viewed`. Resetting the editor does not reset evidence — that's why reveal history is its own table instead of UI state.

notes.title: Self-reported passes earn XP but never mastery
notes.body:
Rubric-graded exercises are passed when the learner sets `selfAssessment === true` and writes a non-empty answer. The grading origin for those attempts is `self_reported`. XP is awarded for an accepted pass, so the learner does get **XP**. But `conceptStatus` throws away any evidence whose origin is `self_reported`, so these passes can never make a concept demonstrated. The tour states both halves together.

Why the others are wrong:
- **nothing until a reviewer approves**: there is no reviewer step; the pass is accepted on the learner's own assessment.
- **mastery only, no XP**: it is the other way round: XP yes, mastery no.
- **both XP and demonstrated after two items**: the origin filter removes self-reported evidence before items are counted.

excerpts.quote: `rubric` grading → `self_reported`: passing requires the learner's own `selfAssessment === true` plus a non-empty written answer.
Self-assessment and assisted passes still earn XP, but they can never demonstrate mastery of a concept.

notes.title: Why different event ids still give XP only once
notes.body:
There are two safety nets, and this question is about the second one. The mutation receipt is looked up by `clientEventId`, so a request with a **new** event id gets no receipt and the handler runs again. What stops a second 10 XP is `award()`: it upserts on the unique `(userId, awardKey)` pair with `update: {}`. The award key for the exercise is the same both times, so the second upsert finds the row and changes nothing. The doc's exercise 2 says your answer must name this constraint, not the receipt.

Why the others are wrong:
- **the receipt replays for both ids**: receipts are matched by event id; a different id has no receipt.
- **an in-memory set per session**: nothing like that exists; the cap is a database constraint.
- **level ignores duplicates when summed**: level is derived from total XP; it does not deduplicate awards.

excerpts.quote: await tx.xpAward.upsert({where:{userId_awardKey:{userId,awardKey}},create:{userId,awardKey,amount,reason},update:{}});
**Check**: your answer names the `(userId, awardKey)` unique constraint, not the mutation receipt.

notes.title: A wrong answer forces Again, whatever button was pressed
notes.body:
The first line of `schedule()` is the one the doc calls the rule juniors miss: `applied = correctness===false ? 'Again' : rating`. A server-graded card that was answered wrongly has `correctness === false`, so the learner's Good is replaced by Again. Again sets the next step to 0 and the delay to 10 minutes. So the card goes to **step 0, due in ten minutes**. The doc's exercise 1 asks this exact case and gives the same answer.

Why the others are wrong:
- **treated like Hard**: Hard is never forced; the override is specifically to Again.
- **Good counts double**: nothing doubles; Easy is the rating that advances two steps.
- **Good stands as given**: that is the mistake the doc warns about; the rating only stands when correctness is null.

excerpts.quote: const applied=correctness===false?'Again':rating; const next=applied==='Again'?0
on a server-graded card, a wrong answer **forces** `Again` no matter which button the learner pressed

notes.title: Why a republished exercise blocks lesson completion
notes.body:
Completing a lesson checks, for each exercise in the lesson, that there is a **passed attempt at the current masteryRevision**. When an exercise is republished with a new revision, the old pass belongs to the outdated version and no longer counts. Until the learner passes the new version, the handler answers `PRACTICE_REQUIRED`. This is step 5 of the tour's first trace.

Why the others are wrong:
- **IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT**: that error is about reusing a `clientEventId` with a different body, not about content changes.
- **old passes carry over**: the trace says a pass on an outdated version does not count.
- **success with 0 XP**: the handler never reaches the award step, because the practice check fails first.

excerpts.quote: loops over the lesson's `exerciseIds` checking each has a **passed attempt at the current `masteryRevision`** — a pass on an outdated version of the exercise does not count (`PRACTICE_REQUIRED` otherwise).

notes.title: What the server checks for browser-run code
notes.body:
For `function-cases` exercises, the code runs in the learner's browser inside the QuickJS runner, and the browser reports which test cases passed. The server does not run the code again. It only checks that the report is well formed and within bounds: at most 25 case ids and a duration up to 60 seconds. That is a trust boundary worth noticing: the server trusts the browser's claim about the results. The attempt is recorded as `browser_automated`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **re-runs every case in QuickJS on the server**: the tour says the browser ran the code and the server checks the report.
- **grades with gradeAnswer**: `gradeAnswer` is used for the third origin, `server_objective`, not this one.
- **stored as self_reported**: `self_reported` is the rubric origin; function-cases attempts are `browser_automated`.

excerpts.quote: `function-cases` grading → `browser_automated`: the browser ran the code in the QuickJS runner and reports which cases passed; the server checks that report's shape and bounds (max 25 case IDs, 60s duration).

notes.title: Same event id, different body: a 409
notes.body:
`mutate()` hashes the operation and body into `requestHash`, then looks up a receipt for this user and `clientEventId`. If a receipt exists, it compares hashes. Same hash: the stored response is replayed. **Different hash: it throws `AppError(409, 'IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT')`**. An event id is a promise that "this is the same request"; changing the body breaks that promise, and the API refuses rather than guess which version you meant.

Why the others are wrong:
- **runs again and overwrites the receipt**: the throw happens before the handler runs; receipts are never overwritten.
- **400 from the strict Zod schema**: strict Zod rejects unknown fields, but a changed valid body passes it; the conflict comes from the hash check.
- **replays the stored response**: replay happens only when the hashes match.

excerpts.quote: if(prior){if(prior.requestHash!==requestHash)throw new AppError(409,'IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT','This event ID was already used with different data.');return prior.response;}
Same event ID with *different* data is a 409 `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`.

notes.title: Why passing a new mastery revision earns XP again
notes.body:
The XP table gives the exercise award key as `exercise:` followed by the item id and the mastery revision. Because the revision is part of the key, a republished exercise with a new revision has a different key. `award()` finds no existing row for that key and creates one, so the learner earns a **new 10 XP**. The doc says it directly: passing a new revision is a new achievement.

Why the others are wrong:
- **20 XP as a lesson**: 20 XP is for lesson completion with a `lesson:` key; an exercise stays an exercise.
- **the key is only the item id**: the documented key includes the revision.
- **revoke and re-grant**: `award()` only ever upserts; nothing deletes or revokes awards.

excerpts.quote: | First accepted exercise pass | 10 | `exercise:<itemId>:<masteryRevision>` |
Note the exercise key includes the `masteryRevision`: if an exercise is republished with a new mastery revision, passing it again is a new achievement.

notes.title: Coverage across runs is not one green run
notes.body:
The integrated test run passed 27 of 28 tests. One assertion was wrong about which denial status the middleware should return; it was corrected, and the affected tests passed on rerun. So every one of the 28 checks has passed in some run. But the record is careful: it does **not** claim a single full-suite run where everything passed at once. Those are different kinds of evidence, because a combined run can expose interactions that separate runs miss.

Why the others are wrong:
- **that any test passed**: it explicitly reports 27 passes on the integrated run.
- **that the protected route returns 401**: it states the canonical protected route still requires exactly 401.
- **that the assertion was ever corrected**: it describes the corrected assertion in detail.

excerpts.quote: All 28 unique checks therefore have passing coverage across these runs; no single all-green full-suite invocation is claimed.
The corrected assertion requires a 401/403/404 denial, an error, and no data; the canonical protected route still requires exactly 401.

notes.title: Hard keeps the step and waits one day
notes.body:
A self-graded card passes `correctness: null`, so the first line of `schedule()` leaves the learner's rating alone: Hard stays Hard. The next line keeps the current step for Hard (`applied==='Hard' ? step`), so the card stays at step 4. The delay line gives Hard a fixed `1440` minutes, which is exactly one day, regardless of the step. Result: **step 4, back in one day**.

Why the others are wrong:
- **reset to step 0 in ten minutes**: that is Again, and Again is only forced when correctness is `false`.
- **advance to step 5 but wait one day**: Hard never advances; Good and Easy do.
- **drop to step 3 for seven days**: the scheduler has no "go back one step" rule.

excerpts.quote: applied==='Hard'?step
applied==='Hard'?1440
**Hard** keeps the current step and waits exactly one day.
